source_text: Verum iam pergamus et ad verba mea, quae de praefatione sublata, sibi impugnanda proposuit: Satis igitur admonuerim, sic istum verba mea quasi refellenda sibi proponere voluisse, ut alibi mediis detractis, sententias interrumperet; alibi extremis non additis decurtaret; et cur hoc fecerit, sufficienter ostenderim. Nunc ad ea quae sicut voluit, nostra proposuit, quae sua posuerit, videamus. Sequuntur enim iam verba eius, et sicut iste insinuavit, qui tibi chartulam misit, prius aliquid de praefatione conscripsit, procul dubio librorum eorum, de quibus pauca decerpsit. Id autem ita sese habet: Doctores, inquit, nostri temporis, frater beatissime, et nefariae, quae adhuc fervet, seditionis auctores, ad hominum, quorum sanctis studiis uruntur, contumelias, et exitium decreverunt per ruinam totius Ecclesiae pervenire; non intellegentes, quantum his contulerint honoris, quorum ostenderunt gloriam nisi cum catholica religione non potuisse convelli. Nam si quis aut liberum in hominibus arbitrium, aut Deum esse nascentium conditorem dixerit, Caelestianus et Pelagianus vocatur. Ne igitur vocentur haeretici, fiunt Manichaei; et dum falsam verentur infamiam, verum crimen incurrunt; instar ferarum, quae circumdantur pinnis, ut cogantur in retia; quibus quoniam deest ratio, in verum exitium vana formidine contruduntur [n176] . Cognosco dicta mea, sed non a te cum integritate prolata; et licet non in his certaminis summa consistat, quia de praefatione sunt; tamen, ut levitas tua liqueat, frater beatissime, in eo loco positum non est, sed in primo statim versu libri. Item cum dixissem: Ad hominum quorum sanctis studiis uruntur, contumelias et exitium; addidi: quoniam iter aliud non patebat, decreverunt per ruinam totius Ecclesiae pervenire. Post quod etiam dixi: Quia liberi confessor arbitrii et Dei conditoris, Caelestianus et Pelagianus vocatur, quo simplices iniquo sermone perterriti, ut ab invidia nominis exuantur, etiam sanam fidem deserunt; credituri procul dubio, nec liberum esse in hominibus arbitrium, nec Deum nascentium conditorem, quando illud, quod prius affirmaverant, utrumque deseruerint. Hoc autem totum a te praetermissum est. Post quod sunt illa quae posuisti, quam sane vera, et quam inexpugnabilia, haud difficilis erit opera comprobare. Nec ego igitur quidquam de tuis dictis minus, nec tu vel primum caput, ita ut a me ordinatum fuerat, rettulisti. Quod ideo inculco, ut gravitas Poeni scriptoris emineat.
pass_a_gloss: But now let us go on also to my words, which taken from the preface he set before himself to be attacked: I would therefore have warned enough, that this man so wanted to set my words before himself as if to be refuted, that in one place with middles drawn out he would interrupt sentences; in another by not adding the extremes he would shorten them; and why he did this, I would have shown sufficiently. Now to those things which as he willed he set forth of ours, let us see what of his he placed. For already his words follow, and as that one insinuated, who sent you the little paper, first he wrote something from the preface, without doubt of those books from which he plucked a few things. But that has itself thus: The teachers, he says, of our time, most blessed brother, and authors of the wicked sedition which still boils, have decreed to come to the insults of humans, by whose holy studies they are burned, and to destruction through the ruin of the whole Church; not understanding how much honor they have conferred on these, whose glory they have shown could not have been torn away except with the catholic religion. For if anyone shall have said either that there is free choice in humans, or that God is the founder of those being born, he is called Caelestian and Pelagian. Lest therefore they be called heretics, they become Manichaeans; and while they fear a false infamy, they incur a true charge; like wild beasts, which are surrounded with feathers, that they may be forced into nets; for whom since reason is lacking, they are thrust by vain fear into true destruction. I recognize my sayings, but not brought forth by you with integrity; and although the sum of the contest does not consist in these, because they are from the preface; nevertheless, that your levity may be liquid, 'most blessed brother' is not placed in that place, but in the first verse of the book at once. Likewise when I had said: To the insults and destruction of humans whose holy studies they are burned; I added: since another way was not lying open, they decreed to come through the ruin of the whole Church. After which I also said: Because a confessor of free choice and of God the founder is called Caelestian and Pelagian, by which the simple, terrified by an unjust speech, that they may be stripped from the ill-will of the name, desert even sound faith; going to believe without doubt, both that there is not free choice in humans, and that God is not the founder of those being born, when they shall have deserted both that which they had first affirmed. But this whole has been passed over by you. After which are those things which you placed, how truly indeed true, and how inexpugnable, the work will not be difficult to prove. Neither I therefore anything less from your sayings, nor you even the first head, so as it had been ordered by me, did you report. Which I therefore stamp in, that the gravity of the Punic writer may stand out.

pass_b_english: Let us now proceed to my words, which he lifted out of the preface and proposed to attack. “I have therefore given sufficient warning that this man chose to set my words before himself for apparent refutation in such a way that in some places he interrupted statements by removing their middle, and in others shortened them by not adding their ending. I have also sufficiently shown why he did this. Now let us see what words of his he set against those of ours that he presented as he wished. For his words now follow. As the person who sent you the sheet explained, he first copied something from the preface, undoubtedly the preface to those books from which he made a few excerpts. It runs as follows: ‘The teachers of our time, most blessed brother, and the authors of the wicked revolt that is still raging, have resolved to reach the abuse and destruction of men whose holy efforts inflame them, through the ruin of the whole Church. They do not understand how much honor they have bestowed on those whose glory they have shown could not be torn down except together with the catholic religion. For if anyone says that human beings have free choice or that God is the Creator of newborn children, he is called a follower of Caelestius and Pelagius. To avoid being called heretics, people become Manichaeans. Fearing a false disgrace, they incur a real crime, like wild animals surrounded by feathers to force them into nets. Lacking reason, they are driven by an empty fear into actual destruction’” (Augustine, On Marriage and Concupiscence 2.6–7).

I recognize my words, but you have not quoted them intact. Although the substance of our dispute does not lie in these words, because they come from a preface, let your carelessness be made plain. “Most blessed brother” is not placed there but in the very first line of the book. Again, after saying, “to reach the abuse and destruction of men whose holy efforts inflame them”, I added, “since no other route lay open, they resolved to do so through the ruin of the whole Church.” After that I also said: “Because anyone who acknowledges free choice and God as Creator is called a follower of Caelestius and Pelagius, simple people, terrified by this unjust language, abandon even sound faith to escape the hatred of the name. They will undoubtedly come to believe both that human beings have no free choice and that God is not the Creator of newborn children, once they have abandoned the two claims they had previously affirmed.” You omitted all of this. After it come the words you quoted; it will not be difficult to prove how true and unassailable they are. I therefore omitted nothing from your statements, while you did not even reproduce the first passage in the order in which I had arranged it. I emphasize this so that the African author's seriousness may stand out.

Freedom to abstain is required for will and sin.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
